title: Flow error handling & retry
scopeHtml: Scope: catch placement, try/catch vs catch, onCompletion, retry/retryWhen with backoff, exception transparency, errors-as-state, stateIn failure, fallback values.

notes.title: What catch really catches
notes.html:
The idea. The catch operator is a net hung UPSTREAM of itself. It catches errors thrown by the flow builder and by operators ABOVE it. It does not catch errors thrown below it, including inside collect { }.

flow { emit(load()) }          // throws here -> caught
    .map { parse(it) }         // throws here -> caught
    .catch { emit(Fallback) }  // net
    .map { render(it) }        // throws here -> NOT caught by the catch above
    .collect { use(it) }       // throws here -> NOT caught

Why. catch wraps the upstream collect in a try/catch and, on exception, runs your block with the throwable and a FlowCollector (so you can emit a fallback). Downstream code runs inside the emit call of upstream, but catch deliberately rethrows downstream exceptions (it checks whether the exception came from the downstream collector; see exception transparency).

try/catch vs catch (Q619).

  • catch operator: recover/fallback for upstream, and you can keep emitting.
  • try/catch around collect: catches everything, including exceptions from the collector body, but the flow is already dead (you can't resume it) and you must be careful not to swallow CancellationException.
  • Use both: catch for expected upstream errors (network) and a try/catch (or CoroutineExceptionHandler) around the terminal operator for bugs in your own collector code. Alternatively move the collector body into onEach above the catch, then use .catch {}.collect(): now it is covered.

Placement bug (Q627). Typical: catch placed first, then a map that throws, so the crash still happens. Or .catch placed BEFORE flowOn/retry it was meant to guard. Rule: catch goes right after the code you want protected and before the part you do not.

Real examples. Retrofit + Room repositories: networkFlow.catch { emit(cachedValue) }. Crashlytics reports of "IOException in collect" usually mean the net was below the failing code or missing.

Analogy. A safety net hung under the trapeze artist: it only catches people who fall from above it, not someone who falls off the roof of the audience seats below.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking catch handles exceptions from collect { }.
  • Placing catch before the operator that throws.
  • Using try/catch around flow { emit() } (see transparency below).

notes.title: onCompletion and exception transparency
notes.html:
onCompletion. Like finally for a flow: runs when the flow completes normally, with an error, or is cancelled. Its lambda receives cause: Throwable?: null on success, the exception on failure or cancellation.

flow.onCompletion { cause -> if (cause != null) log(cause) else hideSpinner() }
    .catch { emit(Error) }
    .collect()

Difference from catch: onCompletion does NOT swallow the exception; it observes it and the exception continues downstream. catch consumes it. It also sees downstream failures (it observes cause from collectors too), and fires on cancellation (cause is a CancellationException). Great for hideLoading().

Exception transparency (Q623). A flow must be transparent to downstream exceptions: if the collector throws, the flow must not catch it and keep emitting. Violation example:

flow {
    try { emit(1) }                 // if collect{} throws, emit() throws HERE
    catch (e: Exception) { emit(2) } // BUG: emitting after downstream failed
}

This breaks the contract and the runtime throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated. The rule: never wrap emit in try/catch inside flow { }; catch only your own producer code (like the network call) and rethrow; or use the catch operator, which handles this correctly. If you must catch, rethrow exceptions that originate from emit.

Real examples. Library authors (Room, DataStore) obey this; the kotlinx.coroutines docs include the exact rule. Teams see the IllegalStateException when porting Rx try { onNext } catch styles.

Analogy. A delivery man (flow) must not open the parcel to hide a defect the customer found; if the customer refuses delivery, the courier cannot pretend nothing happened.

Common interview traps.

  • Wrapping emit in try/catch inside flow { }.
  • Thinking onCompletion handles the error (it only observes).
  • Forgetting onCompletion also runs on cancellation.

notes.title: retry and retryWhen with backoff
notes.html:
The idea. retry re-subscribes to the UPSTREAM when it fails: the flow builder runs again from the top. Whatever was already emitted stays emitted; the retried flow emits again, possibly duplicates.

flow.retry(3) { it is IOException }          // up to 3 retries, only for IOException

retry(retries, predicate) is actually retryWhen { cause, attempt -> attempt < retries && predicate(cause) }. The predicate is a suspend lambda so you can delay inside. Return true to retry, false to rethrow.

Exponential backoff with jitter (Q622).

flow.retryWhen { cause, attempt ->          // attempt starts at 0
    if (cause is IOException && attempt < 5) {
        val base = 500L * (1L shl attempt.toInt())      // 500, 1000, 2000 ...
        delay(min(base, 30_000L) + Random.nextLong(0, 250)) // jitter
        true
    } else false                                         // stop: exception propagates
}

Jitter avoids the thundering herd (a million phones retrying at the same moment after an outage). cause is the exception from upstream; CancellationException is not retried (cancellation is not a failure).

Production incident (Q628). Symptom: backend load spikes during an outage and the app drains battery. Cause: unconditional retry() (infinite, no delay) catches every exception including HttpException 401/400 which will never succeed. Fix: retry only transient errors (IOException, 503), cap attempts, add backoff, surface an error state after the cap.

Re-execution caveats. Retry reruns side effects in the upstream (a POST sent twice). Retried calls must be idempotent. Retry below flowOn/stateIn as needed and upstream of catch, otherwise it never sees the error.

Real examples. Uber/Netflix-style clients use exponential backoff with jitter in their resilience layers; WorkManager has its own BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, which is the persistent counterpart.

Analogy. Redialing a busy phone line: waiting longer between tries (backoff) and at slightly different times than everyone else (jitter) is polite; redialing instantly forever is spam.

Common interview traps.

  • Bare retry() that retries forever and on non-transient errors.
  • Retry on a non-idempotent call.
  • Putting catch upstream of retry so it never sees the failure.
  • Thinking attempt starts at 1 (it starts at 0).

notes.title: Errors as state
notes.html:
The idea. A Flow that throws is terminated: it can never emit again. For a screen, we want "error" to be one of the things you can see, and "retry" to start things again. So model the error as DATA.

sealed interface UiState {
    object Loading : UiState
    data class Content(val items: List<Item>) : UiState
    data class Error(val msg: String) : UiState
}

val state = retryTrigger.onStart { emit(Unit) }
    .flatMapLatest {
        repo.items()
            .map<List<Item>, UiState> { UiState.Content(it) }
            .onStart { emit(UiState.Loading) }
            .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it.message ?: "Unknown")) }
    }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)

catch is INSIDE flatMapLatest so the outer stream survives; the retry button pushes into retryTrigger to restart.

Alternatives. Result<T>/a custom Resource wrapper per emission; or exceptions plus an events channel for one-shot errors (snackbars). Trade-off (Q630): state-with-error is replayed on rotation (a stale snackbar can reappear), so for transient messages use consumed events; for persistent screens use state. Keep cached content on error: Error(cached = items).

Fallback values (Q632). "Show cached data if network fails" is ambiguous: ask whether to show a banner, how stale it can be, and whether to keep retrying. A catch { emit(cached) } is simplest, but silently hides the outage; better emit Content(cached, stale = true).

Real examples. NowInAndroid's Result / UiState sealed classes; Airbnb's MvRx Async<T> (Uninitialized, Loading, Success, Fail) is this idea.

Analogy. A shop sign that says "Closed, back at 3" is better than the shop disappearing from the street.

Common interview traps.

  • Placing catch outside flatMapLatest so one error kills the pipeline.
  • Using a sticky state for a one-time error.
  • Wiping cached content when the refresh fails.

notes.title: Failures in shared flows
notes.html:
The idea. If the upstream of stateIn/shareIn throws, the sharing coroutine (in your scope) dies. The StateFlow keeps the last value but never updates again; and if no handler exists, the app crashes.

What happens exactly (Q625).

  1. Exception propagates from the upstream collect to the sharing coroutine.
  2. That coroutine is a child of viewModelScope; with SupervisorJob siblings survive, but the exception goes to the CoroutineExceptionHandler or uncaught handler, which crashes on Android.
  3. Collectors see nothing. They are not notified; the flow just sits there (frozen UI).

Surviving errors. Put catch (to emit an Error state) and/or retryWhen upstream of stateIn/shareIn. If you want the sharing to resume after the error, wrap with retryWhen so the upstream restarts; the StateFlow stays alive. For hot sources that fail repeatedly, add backoff.

Incident (Q629). Symptom: Crashlytics shows a fatal SocketTimeoutException from viewModelScope with a stack through stateIn; users on bad networks crash right after opening a screen. Cause: no catch before stateIn, Eagerly. Fix: catch + retryWhen upstream; add a test that fakes a throwing repository and asserts an Error state.

Real examples. Many apps fixed "crash on airplane mode toggling" by adding .catch before stateIn.

Analogy. If the only chef at the buffet collapses, the tray just stays cold and nobody tells the diners; you need a backup chef (retry) and a sign (error state).

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming collectors receive the exception.
  • Expecting a retry at the collector to restart the sharing coroutine.
  • Putting catch after stateIn (too late; you can't catch from a StateFlow).

notes.title: Cancellation versus failure
notes.html:
The idea. Cancellation is NOT an error: it is a polite "stop" request, implemented as a CancellationException that travels through suspending calls. Flow operators treat it specially.

Rules.

  • catch does not catch cancellation of the collector: it only handles upstream exceptions; if the flow's own coroutine is cancelled, the operator rethrows. (If the upstream itself throws a CancellationException unrelated to the collector, catch also rethrows to preserve cancellation semantics: since cancelling the collector must never be swallowed.)
  • retry/retryWhen do not retry on cancellation of the collector.
  • onCompletion runs and gets the CancellationException as cause, so you can distinguish.

Breaking cancellation (Q631). The classic bug is catch (e: Exception) (or runCatching) around a suspend call: it swallows CancellationException, so the coroutine continues after being cancelled (leaked work, wasted battery, ViewModel does work after onCleared).

// BUG
try { api.load() } catch (e: Exception) { showError() }
// FIX
try { api.load() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { showError() }
// or: catch only specific types (IOException), or call ensureActive()

runCatching { suspendCall() } has the same problem; rethrow cancellation or avoid it around suspend calls. In finally, suspend calls need withContext(NonCancellable).

Real examples. Bugs in popular open-source apps where cancelling a search left old network calls running; Detekt has SuspendFunSwallowedCancellation for this.

Analogy. If the teacher says "pencils down" (cancellation) and a student keeps writing pretending they didn't hear, that student has swallowed the instruction.

Common interview traps.

  • catch (e: Exception) / runCatching around suspend calls.
  • Expecting retry to retry after the screen is closed.
  • Doing suspending cleanup in finally without NonCancellable.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• catch only guards upstream; use try/catch or move code upstream to cover the collector.
  • onCompletion is finally for flows; catch consumes errors, onCompletion only observes.
  • Never wrap emit in try/catch inside flow { } (exception transparency).
  • retryWhen + capped exponential backoff + jitter, only for transient and idempotent work.
  • Model errors as state inside flatMapLatest so the pipeline survives; shared flows need catch upstream of stateIn.
  • Always rethrow CancellationException.

questions.promptHtml: What does the catch operator on a Flow actually catch? Does it catch an exception thrown inside collect { }?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that Flow operators are declarative and directional (upstream vs downstream), which most candidates get wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: catch only catches exceptions from the flow above it, meaning the producer and every operator placed before it. Anything thrown below it, including inside collect { }, onEach after the catch, or a downstream map, sails past it. So placement is the whole game: put catch as the last operator before collect if you want to guard the whole pipeline, and handle collector-side exceptions with a normal try/catch.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A flow pipeline is a chain of collectors wrapping each other. catch is implemented as a wrapper around the upstream collection: it calls upstream.collect(downstreamCollector) inside a try/catch, but it distinguishes where the exception came from. The implementation (catchImpl) wraps the downstream collector so that if the downstream emit throws, the exception is remembered and rethrown untouched (this is the "exception transparency" rule: a failure in the consumer must not be handled by the producer side). Only exceptions originating upstream reach your lambda.

flow{ } -> map{ } -> catch{ } -> onEach{ } -> collect{ }
  ^ upstream of catch (caught)      ^ downstream (NOT caught)

Other facts you should state:

  • catch does not catch CancellationException caused by the collector's own cancellation (it rethrows if the collecting coroutine is cancelled).
  • Inside the catch lambda you are a FlowCollector, so you can emit(fallback), rethrow, or just log. After the lambda returns, the flow completes normally (the upstream is already dead; catch does not resume it).
  • It catches Throwable, so filter: catch { e -> if (e is IOException) emit(Empty) else throw e }.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
flow { emit(1); error("boom") }
    .map { it * 2 }
    .catch { println("caught ${it.message}"); emit(-1) }   // sees the error from flow{}
    .onEach { if (it == -1) throw IllegalStateException("downstream") } // NOT caught above
    .collect { println(it) }
// prints: 2, caught boom, then crashes with "downstream"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting catch first (right after the builder) and assuming it protects later map calls.
  • Expecting catch to retry or resume the flow. It cannot; upstream is finished.
  • Catching Throwable blindly and masking programmer errors (NullPointerException, IllegalStateException).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you put catch to guard the whole pipeline? → Last, directly before the terminal operator, or use launchIn after it.
  2. Can you emit from inside catch? → Yes, it is a FlowCollector; that is the standard "fallback value" pattern.
  3. Why doesn't it catch downstream exceptions? → Exception transparency: the producer-side must not swallow consumer failures, otherwise a bug in collect would silently turn into a fallback emission.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it's like try/catch for flows." Senior: explains upstream-only semantics via exception transparency, filters by exception type, knows it does not swallow collector cancellation, and knows it terminates the stream.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put .catch before a .map { parse(it) }; a malformed payload crashed the app for 0.8% of sessions because the parse failure was downstream of the catch.

questions.promptHtml: When would you wrap collect in try/catch versus using the catch operator? Can both be used together?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the two tools cover different regions of the pipeline and can pick deliberately.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The catch operator covers upstream only and lets me recover by emitting. A try/catch around collect covers everything: upstream, operators, and my collector lambda, but it ends the collection and can't emit into the flow. I normally use .catch for expected upstream failures (network, IO) and a surrounding try/catch (or a final .catch plus launchIn) when the terminal block itself can throw.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
collect is a suspend function. Exceptions propagate through it like any suspending call, so try/catch works. The difference is what you can do afterwards.

Aspect .catch { } try { collect } catch
Covers upstream yes yes
Covers operators below it no yes
Covers collector lambda no yes
Can emit fallback into flow yes no (flow already dead)
Rethrows cancellation correctly built in you must rethrow CancellationException
Composable in a chain yes no

The classic pitfall with try/catch: catch (e: Exception) also catches CancellationException, which breaks structured concurrency (the coroutine keeps running after being cancelled until the next suspension check).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Both layers, deliberate
try {
    repo.observe()
        .catch { e -> if (e is IOException) emit(Cached) else throw e } // expected failures
        .collect { render(it) }                                          // render may throw
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: Exception) {
    log.e(e)   // collector bug or non-IO failure
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: Exception) swallowing CancellationException.
  • Wrapping a flow { } body in try/catch and emitting inside it (violates exception transparency, see Q623).
  • Using try/catch around launchIn: launchIn returns immediately, so the try/catch protects nothing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does try/catch around viewModelScope.launch { flow.collect {} } work? → Yes, if the try is inside the launch lambda. Outside it, the exception goes to the scope's handler, not your catch.
  2. Why can't I recover and continue with try/catch? → The flow has terminated; you'd have to re-collect, i.e. retry.
  3. How do you handle collector-side exceptions with operator style? → Move the work into onEach before a final .catch, then .launchIn(scope); this is the idiom that makes the catch cover it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks one. Senior layers them, knows cancellation must be rethrown, and moves collector logic into onEach so a single .catch covers it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A try { collect } catch (e: Exception) swallowed cancellation in a ViewModel; after navigation the old collector kept updating a screen that was gone.

questions.promptHtml: What does onCompletion do, and what is the cause parameter? How is it different from catch?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat it as "finally for flows" from people who know it observes but does not handle.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onCompletion { cause -> } runs when the flow ends, like finally. cause is null on normal completion; non-null if the flow failed or was cancelled, and it also reports exceptions that came from downstream. Unlike catch it does not swallow the exception; it keeps propagating after your block. So I use it for cleanup, hiding a loading spinner, or logging, and catch for recovery.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Triggered on: normal completion, upstream exception, downstream exception, cancellation.
  • cause is null only for normal completion. For cancellation it is a CancellationException.
  • The exception continues downstream afterwards, so you still need catch (placed after onCompletion to see it, or before if you want to recover first).
  • Since it is a FlowCollector you can emit a final value on success (e.g. a "done" marker). If cause != null the emit is only reasonable for non-cancellation causes; emitting on a cancelled flow throws.
  • Ordering matters: .catch{}.onCompletion{} -> onCompletion sees null (catch consumed the error). .onCompletion{}.catch{} -> onCompletion sees the exception, then catch handles it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
repo.observe()
    .onStart { loading.value = true }
    .onCompletion { cause ->          // runs for success, error, cancel
        loading.value = false
        if (cause != null && cause !is CancellationException) log.w(cause)
    }
    .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it)) }  // after onCompletion: onCompletion saw the cause
    .collect { render(it) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming onCompletion replaces catch; the app still crashes.
  • Placing catch before onCompletion and then wondering why cause is always null.
  • Emitting a value in onCompletion when cause is a CancellationException.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it run if the collector is cancelled? → Yes, with a CancellationException cause.
  2. Is it the same as try/finally around collect? → Close, but it is composable in the chain and receives the cause; with try/finally you'd reconstruct that with catch blocks.
  3. A StateFlow never completes; does onCompletion ever fire? → Only on cancellation of the collector; the StateFlow itself never completes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it's finally." Senior: explains cause semantics (including downstream failures and cancellation), operator ordering with catch, and the cancelled-emit restriction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A spinner stuck forever because isLoading=false was set only in collect's success path; moving it to onCompletion fixed the error path.

questions.promptHtml: How does retry work on a Flow? What exactly is re-executed, and what does the predicate do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates think retry "resumes" the stream. It resubscribes, which has implications for side effects and for hot flows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: retry(n) { predicate } catches an upstream exception, and if the predicate returns true (and attempts remain), it re-collects the entire upstream from the start. For a cold flow that means re-running the builder (a new network call). Downstream never sees the failure unless retries are exhausted or the predicate returns false, in which case the exception is rethrown. Values emitted before the failure have already reached the collector, so retry can produce duplicates.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Signature (kotlinx.coroutines): fun <T> Flow<T>.retry(retries: Long = Long.MAX_VALUE, predicate: suspend (cause: Throwable) -> Boolean = { true }): Flow<T>. The default is effectively infinite retries with no delay: a tight loop against a failing backend.

Mechanism: retry is built on retryWhen, which wraps the upstream in a loop: collect -> on exception call predicate -> if true, loop and collect again; else rethrow.

Important properties:

  • Upstream only, same as catch. A downstream failure is not retried.
  • Cancellation is not retried (collector cancellation propagates).
  • retry on a hot flow (SharedFlow/StateFlow) is meaningless; they never throw to collectors.
  • Re-collection restarts a cold flow: a flow { emit(api.page(1)); emit(api.page(2)) } that fails on page 2 re-emits page 1 on retry.
  • Use predicate to retry only transient errors (IOException, HTTP 503), never 4xx or programming errors.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
api.prices()                                   // cold flow, new request per collect
    .retry(3) { e -> e is IOException }        // up to 3 re-subscriptions, only transient
    .catch { emit(Prices.Empty) }              // after retries are exhausted
    .collect { render(it) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Bare .retry() = infinite retries without delay; hammers the server and drains battery.
  • Retrying non-idempotent work (POST, payment) since the whole upstream re-executes.
  • Forgetting duplicates when partial emissions happened before failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does retry(3) mean 3 total attempts? → No, 3 retries: up to 4 total executions.
  2. How do you add a delay between attempts? → retryWhen (Q622) or delay inside the predicate.
  3. How do you make retry safe for paged/partial emissions? → Make the upstream idempotent and resumable (track the cursor outside the builder), or scan/distinctUntilChanged downstream to dedupe.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "retry on error." Senior: knows it is re-collection, the infinite default, duplicate partial emissions, idempotency, and that the predicate is for classification.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bare .retry() on an offline-prone call produced ~40 req/s per device during an outage; the backend rate-limited legitimate users.

questions.promptHtml: Implement exponential backoff with jitter for a Flow using retryWhen. What are cause and attempt, and how do you stop retrying?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps need bounded, jittered retry; this checks you can build it and reason about the numbers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: retryWhen { cause, attempt -> } gives me the exception and a zero-based attempt counter. I return true to resubscribe, false to give up and rethrow cause. Inside I can delay, so exponential backoff is delay(min(base * 2^attempt, cap) + jitter), gated by a max attempt count and an "is transient?" check.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
fun <T> Flow<T>.retryWhen(predicate: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(cause: Throwable, attempt: Long) -> Boolean). attempt starts at 0 for the first failure. The lambda is a FlowCollector, so you can even emit a status ("retrying...") before returning true.

Math: base = 500 ms, cap = 30 s: attempts 0..6 give 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 (32 capped) seconds. Total wait over 7 retries ≈ 61.5 s. Without jitter, 10,000 clients that failed at the same instant (a backend blip) all retry in lockstep at t=0.5 s, 1.5 s, 3.5 s... a thundering herd. "Full jitter" picks a random delay in [0, exp], spreading load across the interval.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun <T> Flow<T>.retryBackoff(
    max: Long = 5, baseMs: Long = 500, capMs: Long = 30_000,
    isTransient: (Throwable) -> Boolean = { it is IOException },
): Flow<T> = retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
    if (attempt >= max || !isTransient(cause)) return@retryWhen false
    val exp = minOf(capMs, baseMs shl attempt.toInt())      // 500, 1000, 2000...
    delay(Random.nextLong(exp / 2, exp + 1))                // jitter in [exp/2, exp]
    true
}

shl is safe here because attempt < max; for large max use coerceAtMost on the shift.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning true forever; no max attempts.
  • Shift overflow: baseMs shl attempt overflows Long once attempt reaches ~55 (500 * 2^55 > 2^63 - 1, wraps negative); also shl uses only the low 6 bits of the shift count for Long. Bound attempts or use Math.pow with a cap.
  • Retrying HTTP 4xx, auth failures, or SerializationException.
  • Backoff that ignores connectivity: better to wait for the network callback than burn retries offline.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you surface "retrying (2/5)" to the UI? → emit(UiState.Retrying(attempt)) inside retryWhen before returning true.
  2. How do you test the delays? → runTest with virtual time; advanceTimeBy/currentTime assert the schedule.
  3. Honour a Retry-After header? → Carry it on a custom exception, delay(cause.retryAfterMs) in the predicate, capped.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: delay(1000) fixed. Senior: exponential with cap, jitter, transient-only classification, bounded attempts, overflow awareness, connectivity-aware waiting, and virtual-time tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a 90 s backend incident, fixed 1 s retries from ~200k active clients produced a self-inflicted second outage when the service came back; jittered backoff removed the spike.

questions.promptHtml: What is "exception transparency" in Flow, and what happens if you wrap emit in a try/catch inside a flow { } builder?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the design rule behind catch's behaviour and a common source of IllegalStateException in custom flows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Exception transparency means a flow must not swallow exceptions thrown by its downstream collector. If I wrap emit() in try/catch inside flow { } and swallow the exception, then keep emitting, the runtime throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated. The producer may only catch its own failures (the code that produces values), and must rethrow collector failures. To handle upstream errors, use catch.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why the rule exists: if producers could swallow downstream errors, then flow.map { error() }.collect() could behave differently depending on what produced the values, and operators like take(n) (which cancels the flow via an internal exception) would break. The runtime enforces it in SafeCollector: when emit throws, it records the exception; if the builder later emits again (or completes) after catching it, SafeCollector detects the previous failure and throws the violation error.

Safe pattern: put try/catch around the value-producing code, and emit outside it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: swallows downstream exceptions
fun bad() = flow {
    try {
        emit(load())            // if collector throws here ...
    } catch (e: Exception) {    // ... we swallow it
        emit(Fallback)          // IllegalStateException: exception transparency violated
    }
}

// OK: try only the producing code
fun good() = flow {
    val v = try { load() } catch (e: IOException) { Fallback }
    emit(v)
}

// BEST: let operators do it
fun best() = flow { emit(load()) }.catch { emit(Fallback) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping emit itself in try/catch(Exception).
  • Using try/finally with emit in finally of a cancelled flow (emitting on a cancelled collector throws).
  • Emitting from a different coroutine/context inside flow { } (separate rule: use channelFlow/flowOn; see the buffering chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can I emit in a finally block? → Only if the flow was not cancelled/failed downstream; otherwise it throws. Prefer onCompletion.
  2. How does take(1) stop an upstream? → It throws an internal AbortFlowException that is rethrown through the chain; swallowing it would hang the take.
  3. Is it enforced for channelFlow? → The emission goes through a channel, so the rule is not checked the same way, but you still must not swallow CancellationException.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: knows the exception message exists. Senior: explains the invariant, the SafeCollector check, why take depends on it, and how to restructure code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-written cache-or-network flow { try { emit(net) } catch { emit(cache) } } crashed intermittently only when the UI collector threw during render.

questions.promptHtml: Why do we often model errors as part of the stream's data (UiState / Result) instead of letting the Flow throw? How do you do it for a ViewModel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the principle that a Flow termination is permanent, so long-lived UI streams should not die on a recoverable error.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Flow that throws is finished. For a long-lived UI stream (a screen's state) that is wrong: the user hits a transient error and the screen can never update again. So I convert failures into values: either map the source to a Result/sealed UiState with .map { Success(it) }.catch { emit(Error(it)) } (terminates after the error) or, better, catch inside the per-request unit so the outer stream survives (flatMapLatest { flow{...}.catch{...} }).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two levels of "stream":

  1. The outer, long-lived stream (e.g. query flow -> results). Should never die.
  2. The inner, per-request flow (one network call). It may fail and complete.

Put the catch on the inner flow so the outer keeps going:

queryFlow --flatMapLatest--> [ inner: api.search(q) .map(Success) .catch(Error) ] --> uiState
            outer survives; inner errors become values

Design choices:

  • kotlin.Result<T>: fine for internal layers, but avoid exposing it in public APIs on older Kotlin (Result as a return type was restricted before 1.5); a custom sealed type carries more (Loading, Empty, Error with message and retry).
  • One-shot events (toasts, navigation) are a different problem: they should not live in a replayed state; use a Channel/SharedFlow with consumption semantics or model as consumed state (see the ViewModel/UI-events chunk).
  • Do not leak Throwable into UI; map to domain errors (NoNetwork, Unauthorized, Unknown) so the UI chooses text.
  • Always rethrow CancellationException if you hand-write try/catch.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface UiState {
    data object Loading : UiState
    data class Content(val items: List<Item>) : UiState
    data class Error(val reason: Reason) : UiState
}

val state: StateFlow<UiState> = query
    .debounce(300)
    .flatMapLatest { q ->
        repo.search(q)
            .map<List<Item>, UiState> { UiState.Content(it) }
            .onStart { emit(UiState.Loading) }
            .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it.toReason())) }   // inner catch: outer lives on
    }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting .catch after flatMapLatest on the outer flow: the first error ends the whole screen's stream.
  • Error state replacing content (blank screen) when stale content could still be shown with a banner.
  • Swallowing the error without logging, so Crashlytics never sees it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the retry button go? → It triggers a new value into the outer trigger (e.g. a MutableSharedFlow<Unit> merged into query), re-running the inner flow.
  2. Result vs sealed class? → Sealed class when you need more than success/failure (Loading, Empty, partial).
  3. How to keep showing stale data on error? → scan/runningFold the previous content, or emit Error(previous = lastContent).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: wraps in Result. Senior: distinguishes outer vs inner streams, catches at the inner level, keeps stale content, maps to domain errors, and separates state from one-shot events.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Search screen froze after one 500 response because .catch sat after flatMapLatest; users had to leave the screen to recover.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to a stateIn/shareIn when the upstream flow throws? How do you make a shared flow survive upstream errors?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is a top production killer in MVVM apps; strong candidates know exactly where the exception goes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The upstream is collected inside a coroutine that stateIn/shareIn launches in the scope I passed. An unhandled upstream exception fails that coroutine: it propagates to the scope (in viewModelScope, with no handler it reaches the thread's uncaught-exception handler and crashes the app on Android), and the sharing is dead; the StateFlow just keeps its last value forever. Fix: catch/retry upstream of stateIn. Even then, with Eagerly/Lazily the upstream completed and never restarts; with WhileSubscribed it restarts when subscribers go to zero and come back.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
stateIn calls scope.launchSharing(...), which launches:

scope.launch(context, start) {
    started.command(subscriptionCount).distinctUntilChanged().collectLatest { cmd ->
        when (cmd) {
            START -> upstream.collect(shared)     // exception thrown HERE
            STOP -> ...; RESET_REPLAY -> ...
        }
    }
}

Cases:

  1. No catch upstream: upstream.collect throws -> the launch coroutine fails -> exception goes to the parent. In viewModelScope (SupervisorJob + Main.immediate) the failure does not cancel siblings, but with no CoroutineExceptionHandler the exception is uncaught: crash. If you installed a handler, the app survives but the sharing coroutine is dead; no more updates ever for that ViewModel.
  2. .catch { emit(Error) } upstream: the upstream completes normally after the error value. StateFlow holds the Error. Eagerly/Lazily: finished forever. WhileSubscribed: after the stop timeout with zero subscribers, then a new subscriber, the START command fires again and the upstream is re-collected, giving a natural "retry on next visit".
  3. .retryWhen{} upstream: the sharing coroutine stays alive and the stream recovers by itself.
  4. A StateFlow never completes from the collector's view; after the upstream is gone, collectors just wait.

Also: stateIn(scope) suspend variant (no initial value) throws from the caller's coroutine on first upstream failure before first value; different behaviour.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val prices: StateFlow<UiState> = repo.pricesFlow()                 // may throw
    .map<Prices, UiState> { UiState.Content(it) }
    .retryWhen { e, attempt -> e is IOException && attempt < 5 && run { delay(1_000L shl attempt.toInt()); true } }
    .catch { emit(UiState.Error(it.toReason())) }                  // last resort, upstream of stateIn
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Placing .catch after stateIn; a StateFlow never throws to its collectors, so this catch is dead code and the crash happened inside the sharing coroutine.
  • Believing SupervisorJob prevents the crash. It only stops sibling cancellation.
  • Using Eagerly plus catch, so a single transient error leaves a permanent Error state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does catch after stateIn do nothing? → StateFlow collectors cannot receive upstream exceptions; they surface in the sharing coroutine.
  2. How would you let the user trigger recovery? → Merge a retry trigger into the upstream: trigger.onStart{emit(Unit)}.flatMapLatest{ source().catch{...} }.
  3. How do you test it? → runTest with a source that throws on first collection, backgroundScope for the collector, assert state sequence Loading -> Error -> Content after retry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "add catch." Senior: explains where the exception lands, the crash vs dead-sharing distinction, SharingStarted restart semantics, and puts retry/catch upstream with an inner-flow design.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard went stale for users after a single socket reset because the stateIn upstream died silently with a global handler installed; fixed with retryWhen plus WhileSubscribed.

questions.promptHtml: In catch, retry, and onCompletion, how are CancellationExceptions treated, and how do you avoid breaking cancellation in your own error handling?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Distinguishes people who understand that cancellation is delivered as an exception and must stay cooperative.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cancellation of the collector is not an error these operators handle: catch and retry rethrow it instead of running my lambda or retrying, while onCompletion observes it as a non-null cause. The danger is hand-written code: catch (e: Exception) or runCatching around suspend calls swallows CancellationException, so the coroutine keeps running after being cancelled. I rethrow it explicitly or catch specific types.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• catch implementation: it rethrows if the exception came from downstream, or if it is the cancellation cause of the collecting coroutine's own Job (checked against the coroutine context). So catch { emit(Error) } does not turn a cancelled screen into an Error emission.
  • retry/retryWhen are built on catch; they don't retry a cancelled collection. A CancellationException subclass thrown by upstream code while the collector is still active (e.g. withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException) is, to my understanding of the implementation, caught by catch like any other throwable, since the collector's Job is not cancelled. The trap is elsewhere: hand-written catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } guards rethrow it, and predicates like e is IOException will not match it, so a timeout either escapes or is mistaken for cancellation. Convert it explicitly: catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { throw IOException("timeout", e) }, or use withTimeoutOrNull. (Verify on your coroutines version with a quick test.)
  • runCatching { suspendCall() } catches CancellationException -> must .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }.
  • onCompletion cause non-null for cancellation; clean up there, never launch new suspending work without withContext(NonCancellable).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun <T> safe(block: suspend () -> T): Result<T> = try {
    Result.success(block())
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e                          // never convert cancellation into a Result
} catch (e: Exception) {
    Result.failure(e)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• runCatching in repositories: the most common cancellation leak.
  • Treating TimeoutCancellationException as retryable failure without converting it.
  • Doing cleanup suspend calls in onCompletion / finally after cancel without NonCancellable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is withTimeout inside a flow builder awkward for error handling? → Its exception is a CancellationException subtype, so generic "rethrow cancellation" guards and IOException-based retry predicates both mishandle it; convert it to a domain error.
  2. Is ensureActive() needed in a flow? → Flow builder emit checks cancellation; add ensureActive() in tight CPU loops that don't emit.
  3. How do you lint it? → Detekt SuspendFunSwallowedCancellation rule, code review rule for runCatching over suspend.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "rethrow cancellation." Senior: knows which operators already do it, the TimeoutCancellationException trap, NonCancellable cleanup, and enforces it with lint.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A runCatching around a network call in a repository left zombie requests running after screen exit; battery and data usage spiked until it was linted out.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (1.2M DAU) crashes for 0.6% of sessions on the feed screen. Crashlytics shows kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException from a map in the ViewModel, and the team insists they "already catch errors".

class FeedViewModel(private val api: FeedApi) : ViewModel() {
    val state: StateFlow<FeedUi> = api.feedFlow()          // may throw IOException
        .catch { emit(emptyList()) }
        .map { dtos -> dtos.map { it.toDomain() } }       // throws on a bad payload
        .map<List<Article>, FeedUi> { FeedUi.Content(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, FeedUi.Loading)
}
questions.promptHtml: Find all the problems and fix the code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add try/catch around toDomain." That fixes one symptom, misses that catch is upstream-only, that the error becomes a permanent empty list (hiding failures), and that Eagerly means no recovery.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What should the UI show on network error vs malformed payload? (different handling) Is partial data acceptable? Do we log non-fatals? Are payload failures client bugs or server drift?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move catch to the end so the crash stops; ship as hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) catch is before the throwing map (most likely, matches stack); (b) a new backend field/enum value; (c) null for non-null DTO field; (d) a threading issue (red herring: stack shows no thread problem).
  4. How I'd verify: Crashlytics stack points at toDomain inside the stateIn coroutine; unit test with a malformed DTO using runTest + Turbine.
  5. Root cause: catch only covers upstream (feedFlow). toDomain runs downstream of it, throws inside the sharing coroutine, and goes uncaught to the scope -> app crash. Secondary: emit(emptyList()) turns a network error into "no articles" with no way to retry; Eagerly never restarts the upstream.
  6. Fix:
val state: StateFlow<FeedUi> = api.feedFlow()
    .map { dtos -> dtos.mapNotNull { runCatching { it.toDomain() }.getOrNull() } } // per-item tolerance
    .map<List<Article>, FeedUi> { FeedUi.Content(it) }
    .catch { e ->
        if (e is CancellationException) throw e
        log.nonFatal(e)
        emit(FeedUi.Error(e.toReason()))
    }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), FeedUi.Loading)

Long term: per-item parsing with ignoreUnknownKeys, coerceInputValues, retryWhen for IO errors. (Caveat: runCatching there is non-suspending, so no cancellation issue.) 7. Prevention: a unit test that feeds a malformed item and asserts Content minus bad item; lint: "catch must be last before stateIn/collect"; contract tests on API. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap the whole thing in try/catch(Exception); I wouldn't silently drop whole payloads without a metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the catch must stay first for a reason? → Add a second catch after the map; two catch operators can coexist, each guarding its upstream.
  • What if the crash happens only on Android 8? → Check the red herring: likely server-driven differences in locale parsing; the placement bug is still the cause of the crash.
  • How do you tell network error from parsing error in UI? → Different domain reasons (NoNetwork vs DataCorrupt) from toReason().

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a feed team added a new enum value server-side; old clients without coerceInputValues crashed in a map behind an early catch. The hotfix moved the catch; the lasting fix was tolerant parsing and a canary parsing test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wraps one line in try/catch; misses placement.
  • Hire: identifies upstream-only semantics, moves catch, emits Error state.
  • Strong hire: also fixes Eagerly/recovery, per-item tolerance, logging, tests, and explains the sharing-coroutine crash path.

questions.contextHtml:
Ride-hailing app, 400k concurrent users at peak. At 18:02 the pricing API starts returning 503 for 4 minutes. Backend dashboards show requests/s jump from 3k to 41k, the load balancer starts returning 429, and the outage extends to 19 minutes. Client code shipped last week:

fun fareStream(): Flow<Fare> = api.fares()      // cold flow, one HTTP call
    .retry()                                     // "make it resilient"
    .catch { emit(Fare.Unavailable) }

Logs: HttpException: HTTP 503 repeating roughly every 30 ms per device. Battery-drain complaints rise in the store reviews.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong on the client, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retry(3)." This bounds attempts but keeps no delay: 3 instant retries still triple load, and it retries 4xx too.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the endpoint idempotent (GET)? Does the server send Retry-After? Is there a client-side circuit breaker already? What should the user see during an outage (stale fare vs error)? Is the network layer (OkHttp) also retrying (retryOnConnectionFailure) which multiplies the effect?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side: rate-limit/shed. Client: remote-config kill switch that disables the retry path, and a hotfix build; meanwhile the backend returns Retry-After.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unbounded, undelayed retry() (matches 30 ms cadence); (b) OkHttp retry multiplying; (c) many screens collecting the same flow, each retrying (fan-out); (d) red herring: the catch after retry is fine, it is only reached when retries are exhausted, which with infinite retries is never.
  4. How I'd verify: Charles/OkHttp logging interceptor showing retry cadence; count collectors via a debug counter in onStart; reproduce with MockWebServer returning 503 and runTest virtual time to assert the schedule.
  5. Root cause: retry() defaults: retries = Long.MAX_VALUE, predicate true, no delay. Each failure immediately re-collects the cold flow, issuing a new request. Math: 400k clients x ~33 req/s = ~13M req/s theoretical; the real 41k/s is bounded by connection setup, still 13x baseline. The catch is unreachable in practice, so the user never even sees "unavailable". Synchronized failure also produces a thundering herd on recovery.
  6. Fix:
fun fareStream(): Flow<Fare> = api.fares()
    .retryWhen { e, attempt ->
        val retryable = e is IOException || (e is HttpException && e.code() in listOf(502, 503, 504))
        if (!retryable || attempt >= 4) return@retryWhen false
        val cap = minOf(30_000L, 1_000L shl attempt.toInt())      // 1s,2s,4s,8s
        delay(Random.nextLong(cap / 2, cap + 1))                  // jitter
        true
    }
    .catch { emit(Fare.Unavailable) }                              // now reachable

Long term: honour Retry-After, a shared circuit breaker (open after N failures, half-open probe), single shared upstream via shareIn so N screens do not mean N retry loops. 7. Prevention: Detekt/custom lint banning bare retry(); load test against chaos proxy returning 503; dashboard alert on client-reported retry counts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not retry 4xx or non-idempotent POSTs; I would not put the delay in the UI layer; I would not make retries "smart" without server cooperation (Retry-After).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the endpoint is a POST that creates a ride? → Retry only with an idempotency key; otherwise a retry may double-book.
  • What if the user is offline? → Do not burn retries; wait for connectivity callback (ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback) and then retry once.
  • How would you test the backoff schedule? → runTest, a source failing N times, assert currentTime equals the sum of the delay windows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a recovered backend was knocked over again within seconds by synchronized client retries. Adding jitter and a server Retry-After flattened the recovery curve from a spike to a ramp over ~90 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests retry(3) only.
  • Hire: moves to retryWhen with delay, bounded attempts, transient-only classification.
  • Strong hire: adds jitter and thundering-herd math, idempotency, shared upstream/circuit breaker, connectivity awareness, and lint prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
Trading-watchlist app, 250k DAU. Support reports: "prices freeze after I lose signal in the subway and never recover until I kill the app." No crash reports increase. A global CoroutineExceptionHandler was added last release to "stop the crashes". Code:

class WatchlistViewModel(repo: QuoteRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val quotes: StateFlow<List<Quote>> = repo.streamQuotes()   // websocket-backed callbackFlow
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, emptyList())
}
// viewModelScope created with the app's handler in a custom CoroutineScope factory

Logs: java.net.SocketException: Connection reset once, then silence. UI collectors use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED).
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix; explain why the app does not crash anymore but is stuck.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the websocket on resume." Treats the symptom in the UI layer and misses that the sharing coroutine died.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the websocket flow complete or throw on reset? Is the handler swallowing the exception? Did the freeze start when the handler was added (before, it crashed)? Do other screens share the repo flow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-flag a hotfix that re-creates the ViewModel state on foreground (workaround); let users pull-to-refresh trigger a new collection.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) upstream exception killed the stateIn sharing coroutine (matches single reset + silence); (b) repeatOnLifecycle not restarting: red herring, it restarts collectors but the StateFlow itself has no producer; (c) websocket never reconnects at the data layer; (d) callbackFlow awaitClose missing causing leak.
  4. How I'd verify: Debug-log onCompletion/catch on upstream; coroutine debug agent / DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() showing no running sharing coroutine; reproduce by toggling airplane mode with Eagerly in an instrumented test.
  5. Root cause: stateIn launches the collection in viewModelScope. The SocketException failed that coroutine; before the handler it reached the uncaught handler (crash). With the handler it is logged and swallowed, the coroutine is gone, StateFlow keeps its last value, and with Eagerly nothing ever restarts upstream. The lifecycle-aware collectors are healthy but there is nobody producing.
  6. Fix:
val quotes: StateFlow<QuotesUi> = repo.streamQuotes()
    .map<List<Quote>, QuotesUi> { QuotesUi.Live(it) }
    .retryWhen { e, attempt ->
        if (e !is IOException) return@retryWhen false
        emit(QuotesUi.Reconnecting(attempt.toInt()))      // let the UI show stale + banner
        delay(minOf(30_000L, 1_000L shl attempt.toInt().coerceAtMost(5)))
        true
    }
    .catch { emit(QuotesUi.Failed(it.toReason())) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), QuotesUi.Connecting)

Plus: remove the blanket global handler from this path (it converts loud failures into silent dead state); add connectivity-triggered reconnect. 7. Prevention: Test: source throws once, assert the flow later delivers again; staleness indicator ("last updated 12 s ago") as a user-visible health signal; non-fatal logging for any sharing-coroutine failure. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: WhileSubscribed (5 s) stops the websocket in background (saves battery, but a cold reconnect on return); for a trading app I might keep it alive longer or resubscribe with a snapshot. I would not use a global exception handler as error handling.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did crash reports not increase? → The handler swallowed it; always log inside the handler as a non-fatal.
  • If you keep Eagerly, how do you recover? → retryWhen upstream so the sharing coroutine never ends; there is no restart otherwise.
  • Product wants "last known prices" shown with a stale banner; how? → Keep content in state with a stale flag instead of replacing it with Error.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team "fixed" crash-free-rate by adding a global handler; crash rate dropped 0.4% while support tickets about frozen data tripled. The metric hid a worse failure mode.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames lifecycle or UI collectors.
  • Hire: finds the dead sharing coroutine and adds catch/retry upstream.
  • Strong hire: explains the handler's role, SharingStarted restart semantics, stale-state UX, observability, and test strategy.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing error handling for a banking app's transactions screen (800k DAU). Requirements from product: (1) show cached transactions instantly, then refresh; (2) if refresh fails, keep showing cached data with a dismissible banner; (3) a failed "export statement" action should show a one-time snackbar; (4) auth expiry (401) must navigate to login exactly once, even across rotation. Engineers propose three designs: A) let the Flow throw and catch in the UI; B) wrap everything in Result<T> emitted by the repository; C) sealed UiState with errors as data plus a separate event channel.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you pick and why? Walk through the trade-offs and the implementation shape.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Result everywhere." Ignores that state and one-shot events differ, loses stale data, and mixes layers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the screen be partially loaded (cache OK, network failed)? Are errors retryable? Which errors need analytics? Is there a global 401 interceptor already? Do we support process death?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I'd first write the state table.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (i.e. candidate designs): C with typed errors; B at the data layer only; A rejected.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype one scenario matrix (cache+net ok/fail, 401, rotation, process death) with Turbine tests per design.
  5. Root cause (why A fails): A throwing flow terminates; the screen dies on the first error and loses cached data, and UI-layer catches cannot restart the stream. B: Result is binary, can't express "content + refresh failed", leaks Throwable toward UI, and ordinary Result handling invites swallowed cancellation.
  6. Fix (chosen design):
data class TxUi(val items: List<Tx> = emptyList(), val refreshing: Boolean = false, val banner: BannerError? = null)

private val banner = MutableStateFlow<BannerError?>(null)
private val refreshing = MutableStateFlow(false)

val ui: StateFlow<TxUi> = combine(repo.observeCached(), refreshing, banner) { items, r, b ->
    TxUi(items, r, b)
}.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), TxUi())

fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
    refreshing.value = true
    try { repo.refresh(); banner.value = null }                    // Room emits new items itself
    catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
    catch (e: Exception) { banner.value = e.toBanner() }          // items untouched
    finally { refreshing.value = false }
}

private val _events = Channel<UiEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)       // one-shot
val events = _events.receiveAsFlow()

Rules: domain errors as sealed types (Offline, Unauthorized, Server, Unknown); state carries content plus banner; refresh failure sets banner, never clears items; export failure and 401 go through events (consumed exactly once; Channel buffers while no collector); CancellationException always rethrown; inner .catch around the refresh call, so the outer observation survives. 7. Prevention: State-machine tests; a contract that repositories never throw from a long-lived Flow except cancellation; screenshot tests for banner states; analytics fired in the ViewModel (not UI) once per error. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Channel events can be lost if no collector is active and the buffer is dropped (process death); for must-not-lose navigation (401) I'd model it as persisted state (authExpired = true consumed by the UI) instead. I would not use SharedFlow with replay for events (replays on resubscription), nor a boolean "error shown" flag in the UI.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not StateFlow for the snackbar? → It is conflated and replays the last value; rotation re-shows the snackbar.
  • How do you unit test "banner appears, items stay"? → Fake repo emitting cache then failing refresh; Turbine asserts items unchanged and banner set.
  • Multi-module: where do domain errors map? → Data layer maps exceptions to domain errors; UI maps domain errors to strings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payments screen cleared the list on every refresh error; users believed their transactions had disappeared and flooded support. Keeping content plus a banner removed the ticket class entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one mechanism for everything.
  • Hire: errors as data in a sealed state, content preserved, events separated.
  • Strong hire: addresses inner/outer stream catch, event delivery guarantees, 401 persistence, testing, and layer boundaries.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (600k DAU) has a "sync messages" flow. QA reports: after leaving the chat screen, network sync continues for up to 30 s, and on slow networks the progress spinner sometimes never stops. A staff reviewer flags this snippet:

fun syncFlow(): Flow<SyncProgress> = flow {
    emit(SyncProgress.Started)
    try {
        val msgs = api.fetchMessages()          // suspend, ~2-30 s
        emit(SyncProgress.Fetched(msgs.size))
        db.insertAll(msgs)                       // suspend
        emit(SyncProgress.Done)
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        emit(SyncProgress.Failed(e))
    } finally {
        emit(SyncProgress.Idle)
    }
}

viewModelScope.launch {
    val result = runCatching { syncFlow().collect { _progress.value = it } }
    if (result.isFailure) _progress.value = SyncProgress.Failed(result.exceptionOrNull()!!)
}

Crashlytics: occasional IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated and JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled logged as errors.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only runCatching. Misses emit-in-catch/finally and the transparency violation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is fetchMessages cancellable (OkHttp call cancelled with coroutine)? Is Idle needed on cancel? Who else collects this flow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: rethrow CancellationException in the collector and stop logging cancellations as failures.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) catch (e: Exception) catches CancellationException thrown by fetchMessages on cancel and then emit(Failed) on a cancelled flow -> exception, or the transparency violation when the collector threw; (b) runCatching swallows cancellation, so the coroutine continues the "failed" path after the screen died; (c) finally { emit } on a cancelled flow throws; (d) red herring: the 30 s lag is plain HTTP timeout if the call isn't cancellable.
  4. How I'd verify: Test: collect, cancel after Started, assert no Failed, and Idle handled; check OkHttp Call.cancel via suspendCancellableCoroutine support (Retrofit suspend does this); DebugProbes/logs of onCompletion cause.
  5. Root cause: (1) Catching Exception includes CancellationException. (2) Emitting inside catch/finally in a flow {} after the collector failed or the flow was cancelled is a transparency violation or a cancellation error. (3) runCatching { collect } converts cancellation into a Result.failure, so the code continues running as if a real failure happened, writes state for a dead screen, and logs cancellations as errors. (4) Spinner stuck: finally { emit(Idle) } throws when cancelled, so Idle is never delivered, and the success path relies on it.
  6. Fix:
fun syncFlow(): Flow<SyncProgress> = flow {
    emit(SyncProgress.Started)
    val msgs = api.fetchMessages()
    emit(SyncProgress.Fetched(msgs.size))
    db.insertAll(msgs)
    emit(SyncProgress.Done)
}.catch { e -> emit(SyncProgress.Failed(e)) }       // upstream-only, cancellation-aware
 .onCompletion { _progress.value = SyncProgress.Idle } // runs for success/error/cancel

viewModelScope.launch { syncFlow().collect { _progress.value = it } }   // no runCatching

Here onCompletion sets state directly (a plain assignment, not an emit), which is safe even on cancellation. If a cleanup needs a suspend call, wrap it in withContext(NonCancellable). 7. Prevention: Lint ban on runCatching around suspend code; unit test for cancel mid-flight; review rule: never emit inside try/catch/finally in builders. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch Throwable to be "safe"; I would not swallow cancellation to "keep the spinner consistent"; Idle-on-cancel is a UI concern handled in onCompletion.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if db.insertAll must finish even when the user leaves? → Move it to withContext(NonCancellable) or an application-scoped/WorkManager job; cancelling mid-transaction is safe only if the DB transaction is atomic.
  • Why does the exception message say StandaloneCoroutine? → That is the launch job being cancelled when the ViewModel clears; a normal event, not an error.
  • Would try/catch outside collect be wrong? → Fine if it rethrows CancellationException; the operator form is cleaner and composable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a sync spinner was permanently stuck for ~2% of users because emit(Idle) lived in finally and threw on cancel; moving it to onCompletion removed the class of bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes only runCatching.
  • Hire: spots emit-in-catch/finally, replaces with catch+onCompletion.
  • Strong hire: explains the transparency check and cancellation mechanics, NonCancellable cleanup, persistence of must-finish work, and tests for cancel.

questions.contextHtml:
Product writes: "If the network fails, show something useful instead of an error." The screen is a product-detail page (2M DAU, median 3G-ish users in some markets, p95 API latency 2.8 s, failure rate ~4%). Existing code:

fun product(id: String): Flow<Product> = flow { emit(api.product(id)) }

The team debates: emit a default empty product? Emit cached copy? Emit nothing? One engineer proposes .catch { emit(Product.EMPTY) }, another .onEmpty { emit(cached) }.
questions.promptHtml: How do you clarify and implement "fallback values"? What are the pitfalls of each operator?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: catch { emit(Product.EMPTY) } immediately: shows a blank/zero-price product, which is worse than an error (wrong price on a purchase page).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is "useful" here: stale cache, a skeleton, or a partial page? How stale may data be (price/stock)? Should the user be told it is stale? Which errors qualify (offline vs 5xx vs 404)? Can the user purchase from stale data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; first agree a fallback matrix with product.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): (a) cache-then-network with stale flag; (b) cache only on transient errors, error UI on 404/401; (c) placeholder defaults (only for non-critical fields).
  4. How I'd verify: Test matrix: network ok / IO error / 404 / empty body, with and without cache, using fakes and Turbine; check that price shown on checkout always comes from fresh data.
  5. Root cause (of the pitfalls): catch { emit(x) } replaces the stream after an error and then completes: no further updates. onEmpty triggers only if the flow completes without emitting any item; it does not fire on errors. onStart { emit(cached) } shows cache first but doesn't distinguish stale from fresh. A default object conflates "no data" with "valid data".
  6. Fix:
sealed interface ProductUi {
    data object Loading : ProductUi
    data class Fresh(val p: Product) : ProductUi
    data class Stale(val p: Product, val reason: Reason) : ProductUi
    data class Error(val reason: Reason) : ProductUi
}

fun productUi(id: String): Flow<ProductUi> = flow {
    val cached = dao.get(id)
    if (cached != null) emit(ProductUi.Stale(cached, Reason.Refreshing))
    emit(ProductUi.Fresh(api.product(id).also { dao.upsert(it) }))
}.retryWhen { e, a -> e is IOException && a < 2 && run { delay(500L shl a.toInt()); true } }
 .catch { e ->
    val cached = dao.get(id)                                  // a fresh read inside catch
    if (cached != null && e is IOException) emit(ProductUi.Stale(cached, e.toReason()))
    else emit(ProductUi.Error(e.toReason()))
 }

(Note: the try is not inside the builder around emit; the operator form respects exception transparency.) Disable checkout when the state is Stale. 7. Prevention: Tests per matrix cell; analytics on stale-served rate; a TTL on cache; lint against fake default domain objects. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not fabricate default values for price/stock; I would not hide staleness from the user; offline-first with Room as the single source of truth is a bigger change and is the long-term answer, but not necessary to fix this ticket.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• When does onEmpty apply here? → A search/list flow that completes with zero items; use it to emit an Empty state, not to handle errors.
  • Why read the DB again inside catch? → The earlier cached is local to the builder and out of scope; also it may have been updated in between.
  • Two emissions race with flatMapLatest on a rapid id change? → The latest wins; the stale emission for the old id is cancelled.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an app displayed a "0.00" fallback price after API timeouts, and a few users tried to buy at that price; the incident review banned fabricated defaults and introduced explicit Stale states.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: emits a blank default on any error.
  • Hire: clarifies requirement, cache fallback via catch, distinguishes onEmpty.
  • Strong hire: explicit Fresh/Stale/Error modelling, error classification, checkout gating, retries, and a test matrix.
